strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK increase causes register spill and occupancy drop
strategy_description: Adding a @triton.autotune decorator to increase XBLOCK (from 128 to 512–2048) caused the compiler to allocate more registers per thread (28→34), which reduced Block Limit Registers from 16 to 12 and dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 76.5% to 63.3%. The larger tile also increased total executed instructions by ~38% (4.2M→5.8M), and elapsed cycles grew from 13,688 to 19,883, resulting in a 44% slower kernel. When the original kernel is already register-constrained near the block-limit boundary, increasing XBLOCK can push register usage over a threshold that reduces SM occupancy enough to outweigh any partial-wave or latency-hiding benefit.
fast_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (faster)
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:]
    # same body

grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](..., xnumel, XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Kernel already has high theoretical occupancy (≥100%) with current XBLOCK; registers_per_thread is low (≤28) and Block Limit Registers is high (≥16); partial-wave overhead is the primary bottleneck.
do_not_apply_when: Registers per thread are already near or above the threshold where increasing XBLOCK would reduce Block Limit Registers (e.g., 28 regs/thread where autotune configs cause compiler to allocate 34+ regs, dropping block limit from 16 to 12 and theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75%). Also avoid when the grid lambda is not updated to use meta['XBLOCK'] — a fixed grid with autotune produces incorrect wave counts.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune changes the constexpr XBLOCK value seen by the compiler, which can alter register allocation even if the kernel body is unchanged. The grid must be a lambda using meta['XBLOCK'] when autotuning XBLOCK; using a fixed grid (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128)) with autotune is also a bug — the grid does not adapt to the selected XBLOCK. In CUDA, the equivalent risk is that larger thread blocks increase register pressure and reduce SM occupancy.

strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK increase causes register spill and occupancy drop
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512–2048) caused the compiler to allocate more registers per thread (28→34), which reduced the register-limited block count per SM (Block Limit Registers: 16→12) and dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 76.5% to 63.3%. The increased instruction count (4.2M→5.8M executed instructions) combined with lower occupancy extended kernel duration from 9.28µs to 13.22µs. When the original kernel is already register-constrained near the block limit boundary, introducing autotune with larger tile sizes can push register usage over a threshold that reduces occupancy more than the tile-size benefit provides.
fast_pseudocode:
# BEFORE (faster)
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # 28 regs/thread, Block Limit Registers=16, 100% theoretical occupancy
    ...
grid = (triton.cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](..., xnumel, XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Kernel is already near the register block limit boundary (Block Limit Registers close to Block Limit Warps); adding autotune with larger XBLOCK configs causes register pressure increase that reduces theoretical occupancy
do_not_apply_when: Kernel has significant register headroom (registers_per_thread well below the threshold that would reduce Block Limit Registers); in that case, larger XBLOCK autotune may legitimately help by eliminating partial waves and improving ILP
framework_notes: Triton-specific: @triton.autotune changes the compilation context in a way that can increase register allocation even when the kernel body is unchanged, because the compiler may make different spilling decisions for larger constexpr tile sizes. Always check registers_per_thread and Block Limit Registers before and after adding autotune. The grid lambda must match the autotuned XBLOCK (use lambda meta: (cdiv(n, meta['XBLOCK']),)) but the original code left the grid hardcoded to cdiv(n, 128), which is a secondary bug but not the root cause of the regression.

strategy_title: Autotune XBLOCK Increase Causes Register Spill Regression
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK configs (512, 1024, 2048) caused registers per thread to increase from 28 to 34, reducing Block Limit Registers from 16 to 12 and dropping theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 76.5% to 63.4%. The increased register pressure also inflated executed instructions by ~38% (4.2M to 5.8M), extending kernel duration from 9.28µs to 13.09µs despite the autotune overhead being amortized. The partial-wave tail (LaunchConfiguration rule, 20% potential speedup) was not the binding bottleneck; the register file constraint was, and enlarging tiles made it worse.
slow_pseudocode:
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # XBLOCK=128, 28 regs/thread, 100% theoretical occupancy
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    ...

grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)
applicable_when: Kernel has a large partial-wave tail (LaunchConfiguration rule >15% speedup_pct), low register usage per thread (well below block register limit), and no shared memory constraints. Autotune overhead is amortized over many invocations.
do_not_apply_when: Registers per thread are already near the block register limit (e.g., 28 regs/thread with Block Limit Registers=16 at 100% theoretical occupancy). Increasing XBLOCK in autotune configs causes the compiler to allocate more registers (due to larger live ranges across the wider tile), which reduces Block Limit Registers and drops theoretical and achieved occupancy, increasing total instruction count and kernel duration. Avoid when theoretical occupancy is already at 100% and register budget is tight.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK values can cause the compiler to allocate more registers per thread because wider tiles create larger live variable ranges. This is a Triton-specific compiler behavior. Always check that the register count does not increase when adding autotune configs with larger tile sizes. The equivalent concern in CUDA is that larger thread block sizes or more work per thread can increase register usage and reduce occupancy.

strategy_title: Autotuning larger XBLOCK increases register pressure, hurts occupancy
strategy_description: Adding @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK values (512–2048) caused the compiler to allocate more registers per thread (28→34), which reduced Block Limit Registers from 16 to 12 and dropped theoretical occupancy from 100% to 75% and achieved occupancy from 76.5% to 63.3%. The increased register pressure more than offset any partial-wave tail elimination benefit, resulting in 41% more elapsed cycles (13688→19480) and 38% more executed instructions (4.2M→5.8M), producing a 0.71x regression. When a kernel is already near 100% theoretical occupancy with a small register footprint, forcing larger tiles via autotune can silently increase register usage and destroy occupancy.
slow_pseudocode:
# BEFORE: fixed small tile, low register pressure, high occupancy
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # kernel body
    ...

# call site
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # 9800 blocks, 4.64 waves/SM
kernel[grid](..., XBLOCK=128)  # 28 regs/thread, 100% theoretical occupancy
fast_pseudocode:
# AFTER (regressed): autotune with larger tiles, higher register pressure
@triton.autotune(
    configs=[
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 512},  num_warps=4),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 512},  num_warps=8),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1024}, num_warps=4),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 1024}, num_warps=8),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 2048}, num_warps=8),
        triton.Config({'XBLOCK': 2048}, num_warps=16),
    ],
    key=['xnumel'],
)
@triton.jit
def kernel(..., XBLOCK: tl.constexpr):
    # same kernel body
    ...

# call site
grid = (cdiv(xnumel, 128),)  # grid still hardcoded to 9800!
kernel[grid](...)  # autotune picks larger XBLOCK but grid not updated -> 34 regs/thread, 75% theoretical occupancy
applicable_when: Kernel has a partial-wave tail AND register pressure is low (≤24 regs/thread) AND theoretical occupancy is already below 80% so register increase cannot hurt further.
do_not_apply_when: Kernel already achieves near-100% theoretical occupancy with its current register count (≤32 regs/thread at block_limit_registers=16); in this regime, larger XBLOCK tiles increase register allocation, reduce block_limit_registers, and drop theoretical occupancy, causing net regression. Also avoid when the call-site grid is not updated to use meta['XBLOCK'] — the autotune will select a larger XBLOCK but the grid remains sized for the original small XBLOCK, wasting work.
framework_notes: In Triton, @triton.autotune with larger XBLOCK values causes the compiler to unroll more loop iterations and spill into more registers. The call site grid must also be updated to lambda meta: (cdiv(xnumel, meta['XBLOCK']),) — in this case the grid was NOT updated (still hardcoded to cdiv(xnumel, 128)=9800), compounding the regression by keeping the same number of blocks while each block did more work with higher register pressure.
